newsitem.title: USA: United Airlines proposes safety pact.
newsitem.headline: United Airlines proposes safety pact.

text.p: UAL Corp's United Airlines hopes to strike a pact with its code-share partners that would require all the carriers to agree to certain safety standards, a top officer said Tuesday.

Edmond Soliday, United's vice president for safety and security, told Reuters United has sent a proposal to its four major code-share partners: Deutsche Lufthansa AG, Thai Airways International, SAS Norge ASA, and Air Canada.
"Every one is open to discussion of the issue," he said.
"We have to develop standards that go beyond regulation. Safety is more than regulatory compliance," Soliday told Reuters after his speech at the International Airline CEO conference here.

He said safety standards can be condensed to a list of about 25 items such as: internal audit standards, a policy to follow up on regulatory or company-discovered safety violations and protection for whistle-blowers.
Soliday could not say when such an agreement with code-share partners might be struck.
He emphasized that United would not impose its standards on any other airline. "As to the rules of the road, we will try to mutually agree," he said.

Code-share marketing agreements allow airlines to ticket passengers on the planes of their partners. United has always said carriers must adopt more stringent safety standards than those mandated by government.
Soliday said the same sort of safety agreements will also be struck with the express carriers United works with in the United States.
The six carriers, which United calls United Express, have a marketing agreement to provide feeder service from smaller markets into United's domestic hubs.

He noted that United has also worked with governments and unaffiliated airlines to improve safety standards. Last summer United lent employees and gave its safety books to Servivensa Airlines in Venezeuela. United also lent United employees to Uruguay in January as that country prepared for an international safety audit.
"This experience has been positive and we would do it again tomorrow," he said.
Soliday said United would take a cooperative stance toward a code-share partner that was found to be deficient in the mutually conceived safety standards.
